1.text:
'Alif-Lãm-Mĩm' is the full wording of this verse, three letters at the start of Surah Al-Imran. One view leaves their meaning with Allah alone. Another sees the disconnected letters as a challenge because the Qur'an is built from letters used in ordinary Arabic speech, yet its hearers cannot bring a book like it. This reading links the opening to the form of revelation rather than assigning a certain word to each letter. A spiritual reading treats the letters as allusions about sufficiency, kindness, and harmony. A source also preserves a report about the delegation of Najran and an oath affirming Allah’s oneness. These are distinct explanations, and the verse itself does not spell out a single lexical definition. The opening also belongs to the sequence of revelation after Al-Baqarah. The prayer at the end of Al-Fatihah asked for guidance to the straight path, and the account at the beginning of Al-Baqarah presents the Qur'an as that guidance. Al-Imran begins within the same discussion of the Book, while the surah's following verses move to Allah's Oneness and the scriptures revealed before the Qur'an. The short opening therefore marks the beginning of a new surah without closing the question of what each letter means.

**What the Letters Mean.**

Alif Lām Mīm God knows best what He means by these letters. It is said that by listening to these disconnected letters [Alif Lām Mīm] which are contrary to the ordinary customs of human discourse every concept disappears from the hearts whether it be a known written cus tomary or imagined thing and whether it arises from necessity Ḍarūra sensory perception ḥiss or independent reasoning ijtihād.

**Letters in the Qur’an.**

Alif Lām Mīm – the placement of such letters has been discussed at the beginning of Sūrah Al-Baqarah. They indicate the inability of the Arabs to bring a Qur’ān like this one despite the fact that it is composed of letters similar to the ones at the beginning of this Sūrah, which also form the parts of their own speech.

**What the Letters Allude To.**

Alif Lām Mīm His saying Alif alludes to His being sufficient for you in all of your states. He is the One who sets in motion what restores you and is solely sufficient for you in what helps you. Without your asking-and even without you knowing your own state-He suffices for you even if you do not perceive it. The Lām alludes to His kindness luṬf to you at the most subtle and hidden level so much so that the locus of favor by which He strengthens you is not apparent to you. The Mīm alludes to the harmony muwāfaqa of the stream of the [divine] determination of events taqdīr with the circumstances requested by the friends.

**Guidance from Earlier Surahs.**

It will be recalled that at the end of the Surah Al-Fatihah a prayer for guidance to the straight path was made. After that, by be-ginning the Surah Al-Baqarah with 1 ‌ (This Book which has no doubt in it), it was pointed out that the prayer made in Su-rah Al-Fatihah for guidance to the straight path has been accepted and Allah Almighty has sent down this Qur'an which provides guidance to the straight path.

**Guidance and Book.**

He has sent guidance for man throughout the ages, including the Torah and the Bible, which were revealed to the former prophets. Ultimately, in accordance with God’s plan, the final book in the form of the Quran was sent down to man. The Quran is not only a genuine book of guidance but also serves as the criterion or standard of right and wrong.

**Allah and an Oath.**

And on his authority he related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: (Alif. Lam. Mim.) that he said: 'Allah informed us about the story of the delegation of Najran; it is also said that this is an oath by which Allah swore that He is One and that He has neither progeny nor partner. (Alif-Lam-Mim. Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists.)

2.text:
'Allah! There is no god worthy of worship except Him, the Ever-Living, All-Sustaining' begins with absolute oneness and states that worship belongs to Allah alone. 'the Ever-Living' rules out death and deficiency, and 'All-Sustaining' names the One who exists without dependence and sustains every created thing. The attributes explain why none besides Him deserves worship. They are not only names but the basis of the declaration. The verse gives no partner or rival a share in worship, and it presents the Creator as the One on whom the whole creation depends. The following verse speaks of the Book revealed in truth, so the statement about Allah's life and sustaining power introduces the One who sends revelation and guides. 'There is no god' excludes every object of worship other than Him, while 'except Him' makes the affirmation exclusive. The names Ever-Living and All-Sustaining provide connected grounds for that exclusivity. He does not die or diminish, and His creation remains in need of Him. All creation remains dependent on Him, while He needs nothing from creation. The attributes describe the One who is self-subsisting and sustains creation, with no death or deficiency.

**The Ever-Living and Sustainer.**

In the words (Allah: there is no god but He) which follow immediately, the doctrine of the Oneness of Allah has been put forth as a categorical declaration. (Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists) and,. (Allah! There is no God save Him, the Alive) Who dies not and is not evanescent, (the Eternal) the Self-subsistent Who has no beginning. Then come the words (the Alive, the All-Sustaining) which lay out a rational proof of the Oneness of Allah. The only Being worthy of worship is the One who has always been Alive and Present and shall always live and sustain.

**Worship Belongs to Him.**

It means that there is absolutely nothing worthy of worship other than Allah. (Alif-Lam-Mim. Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists.) Therefore, it is crystal clear that all things in this world which have no power to come into being by themselves, nor can they sustain it - be they idols carved in stone, or water, or trees, or angels and apostles - none of them is worthy of worship. Allah is the One Who alone deserves to be worshipped. Bowing to the truth required them to bow to the Prophet and to God, and they thought that by surrendering to the Supreme Being and His Prophet they would diminish in stature.

**The Book That Follows.**

(It is He Who has sent down the Book to you with truth,) means, revealed the Qur'an to you, O Muhammad, in truth, meaning there is no doubt or suspicion that it is revealed from Allah. (In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)(1. Alif-Lam-Mim.)(2. Allah! None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One Who sustains and protects all that exists.)(3. It is He Who has sent down the Book to you with truth, confirming what came before it. And He sent down the Tawrah and the Injil,)(4. Aforetime, as a guidance to mankind. And He sent down the criterion. Truly, those who disbelieve in the Ayat of Allah, for them there is a severe torment; and Allah is All-Mighty, All-Able of Retribution.)

3.text:
'He has revealed to you O Prophet the Book in truth' identifies the Qur'an as revelation from Allah, free of doubt and suspicion. 'confirming what came before it' ties it to earlier revealed books, rather than presenting it as an isolated message. 'as He revealed the Torah and the Gospel' names the earlier revelations given to Moses and Jesus. The verse grounds continuity among the prophets and their scriptures. In this context, the reference is to the original Torah and Gospel revealed to those prophets, and the Qur'an confirms their divine origin. It does not claim that the final scripture has no distinct law or teaching. The following verses continue the argument by identifying the revelation's guidance and distinguishing truth from falsehood. The point here is that the Book sent to Muhammad stands in the same line of divine revelation as the Torah and Gospel. Allah's message is not new in its call to His oneness, even though each revelation came in its own time. The verse moves from the Book's source, to its relation with what preceded it, and then to two named scriptures as examples of that continuity.

That is to say Even though We revealed Our books to the messengers before you We did not omit the remembrance dhikr of you from any book. 5.text:
'Surely nothing on earth or in the heavens is hidden from Allah' leaves no place outside His knowledge. The verse names both earth and heaven and states that nothing in either is hidden. Its claim includes what people see and what they cannot see; Allah's knowledge is not bounded by human perception. It follows the account of revelation and the Standard: the One who sends guidance knows what is hidden from His servants and what they need. The next verse turns from what is hidden to Allah's shaping of people in the wombs as He wills. That sequence connects knowledge with creation; no hidden breath or unseen need is beyond Him. A servant may need what no one else perceives, but that need is not hidden from the One who creates and sustains all things. Even a breath is counted, and knowledge reaches before birth and after death, beyond what another person can observe. Allah's knowledge includes what is visible and what is hidden, and it is not limited by the senses.

**God's Knowledge of Heaven and Earth.**

Nothing no existent thing whatever is hidden in heaven and earth from God on account of His knowledge of universals and particulars. God specifies them heaven and earth because sensory perception does not go beyond these. Allah states that He has perfect knowledge in the heavens and earth and that nothing in them is hidden from His watch. He knows everything, whether it is open or hidden. Only God can truly tell us what He is in His Being and in His attributes. Not a particle exists in the heaven and earth unless He is its originator and creator mubdiʿ hi.

**Before Birth and After Death.**

And He has made this so clear in His Book, that any reader who is eager for knowledge of Him will certainly gain enlightenment from it. The right course of action for man can be determined only by a Being who has not only known man from his birth to his death, but also knows what has gone before his birth and what will happen after his death. It is, therefore, only God who, after placing the nature of man in the perspective of the entire universe, may decree what kind of conduct will guarantee man’s success in this world and the next, for a sound human mentality can only be one which is in harmony with the rest of the world and in complete accord with the vaster system of the cosmos. It is only God who has the power and the knowledge to ordain what it befits human beings to strive for in the present world. This being so, the only realistic approach for man is to trust in His Maker and accept and follow His guidance wholeheartedly and with full confidence. A servant does not breathe a single breath without God counting it muḥṣīhi.

**Creation in the Womb.**

Verse 3 which follows carries the reported proof of the Oneness of Allah. Truly, nothing is hidden from Allah, in the earth or in the heaven He it is Who shapes you in the wombs as He wills. (He it is Who shapes you in the wombs as He wills.) meaning, He creates you in the wombs as He wills, whether male or female, handsome or otherwise, happy or miserable. This Ayah refers to the fact that 'Isa, son of Mary, is a created servant, just as Allah created the rest of mankind. Allah created 'Isa in the womb (of his mother) and shaped him as He willed. Therefore, how could 'Isa be divine, as the Christians, may Allah's curses descend on them, claim? 'Isa was created in the womb and his creation changed from stage to stage, just as Allah said,.

7.text:
'He is the One Who has revealed to you, O Prophet, the Book' identifies the One who sends revelation and the messenger who receives it. 'of which some verses are precise' points to clear statements whose meaning is established. 'they are the foundation of the Book' makes those verses the basis for reading the rest. 'while others are elusive' acknowledges passages whose full meaning is not immediately clear. 'Those with deviant hearts follow the elusive verses seeking to spread doubt through their false interpretations' shifts attention to the way a reader handles uncertainty: the aim is discord, not guidance. 'but none grasps their full meaning except Allah' sets a limit on what people can claim to know. Readers differ over the pause here: some stop at Allah, while others connect the well-grounded in knowledge with what follows. 'As for those well-grounded in knowledge, they say' introduces a response of humility rather than pursuit of confusion. 'We believe in this Quran' and 'it is all from our Lord' affirm the whole revelation, not only what is easy to understand. 'But none will be mindful of this except people of reason' closes by linking reflection with sound understanding. The verse does not license ignoring difficult passages; it directs interpretation back to the clear foundation and calls for faith where the full reality remains beyond human knowledge. The discussion also marks a limit: uncertainty is not permission to reject what the clear verses establish. One reading leaves the full interpretation with Allah alone; another joins those well-grounded in knowledge to the response that follows. In either case, the following words affirm that all the verses are from their Lord, and people of reason take admonition. The clear verses remain the reference point; interpretations of an elusive phrase that contradict them are rejected. Some readings call certain passages allegorical or leave their full reality to Allah, while the grounded affirm the entire Book. This restraint protects the message and the reader from turning uncertainty into discord. The following verse turns that posture into a prayer for hearts to remain firm.

**Clear Verses as the Foundation.**

He it is Who revealed to you the Book wherein are verses that are clear lucid in proof forming the Mother Book the original basis for rulings and others allegorical whose meanings are not known such as the opening verses of some sūras. Allah Almighty has called the first kind of verses, that is, the Muhkamat Umm al-Kitab ' (which has been translated literally as 'mother verses') meaning thereby that such verses are the very root and essence of all teachings, and the meanings and explanations of which are free of doubt or ambiguity. (He it is Who hath revealed unto thee (Muhammad) the Scripture) who sent you Gabriel with the Scripture (wherein are clear revelations) expositing the lawful and unlawful which are not abrogated and which are acted upon. (They are the substance of the Book) they are the foundation of the Book as they are the leading theme in each book. The first are clear revelations, quite precise in their meaning, since they have been couched in a direct style. O Prophet, He is the One Who revealed to you the Qur’ān, which contains verses with clear and unambiguous meaning, and these represent the majority of the Book and are the reference point when there is disagreement. He it is who has sent down upon thee the Book, wherein are firm verses, which are the mother of the Book, and others ambiguous.

**Unclear Verses and Their Limits.**

He God refers to the whole Qur’ān as 1 ‘clear’ muhkam where He says A Book whose verses have been made clear Q. 111 meaning that it contains no imperfections; and as 2 ‘allegorical’ mutashābih where He says A Book consimilar Q. 3923 meaning that its parts resemble each other in terms of beauty and veracity. Through this verse, Allah Almighty has put an end to these doubts by saying that such expressions are in the category of Mutashabihat where the outward meaning is not intended; they are, rather, a secret between Allah and His Messenger, the reality of which cannot become manifest to others for whom it is not even appropriate to go about determining the possible meanings of these words. Since the exact intention of the second kind of verses, that is, the Mutashabihat remains ambiguous and uncertain, therefore, the correct method of their interpretation would be to harmonize them with the first kind, that is, the Muhkamat . Then, the rule is that any interpretation of the Mutashabihat which goes against the first kind should be rejected absolutely and only that interpretation should be given credence which is not against the verses of established meaning (Muhkamat). (And others (which are) allegorical) vague in their meanings to the Jews, like the use of the letters of the alphabet according to their numerical value (hisab al-Jumal) in such instances as Alif. Ra; it is also said that (others (which are) allegorical) means: other verses that are abrogated and no longer acted upon. There are two kinds of subjects dealt with in the Quran, one pertaining to the known human world, like historical events, signs from the universe and commandments for worldly life; the other pertaining to unseen matters which are not comprehensible by man in this life, for instance, God’s attributes, and the states of Heaven and Hell, etc. The second relate to the unknown world (for man) and cannot, therefore, be expressed in everyday language. That is why they are framed in an allegorical style. For instance, if we say, ‘man’s hand’, this is an example of the expression of a fact, but if we say, ‘God’s hand’, this is an example of an allegory. Those who do not understand this difference fall into the error of interpreting allegorical verses quite literally. It also contains other verses that may have more than one meaning and are puzzling for most people. They interpret the unclear verses according to the clear ones.

**Hearts Seeking Doubt and Discord.**

As for those in whose hearts is deviation inclination away from truth they follow the allegorical part desiring sedition among the ignorant of them throwing them into specious arguments and confusion and desiring its interpretation its explanation and none knows its interpretation its explanation save God Him alone. (they follow that which is not entirely clear thereof) meaning, they refer to the Mutashabih, because they are able to alter its meanings to conform with their false interpretation since the wordings of the Mutashabihat encompass such a wide area of meanings. (But those) the Jews Ka'b Ibn al-Ashraf, Huyayy Ibn Akhtab and Judayy Ibn Akhtab (in whose hearts is doubt) scepticism, opposition and deviance from guidance (pursue, forsooth, that which is allegorical seeking) in the Qur'an ((to cause) dissension) pursuing disbelief, ascribing partners to Allah, and holding fast to the error they are in (by seeking to explain it) to determine the future of this nation so that dominion reverts back to them. Those who seek other than the truth leave the clear verses and focus on the unclear ones, trying to create doubts and mislead people, and interpret them to suit their corrupt views. " He also said, "As for the unclear Ayat, they can (but must not) be altered and changed, and this is a test from Allah to the servants, just as He tested them with the allowed and prohibited things. (When you see those who follow what is not so clear of the Qur'an, then they are those whom Allah described, so beware of them.)"

**Who Knows the Meaning?.**

'They say, “Our Lord!”' begins a supplication, not a claim that the well-grounded can keep themselves firm without help. 'Do not let our hearts deviate after you have guided us' asks Allah to maintain the guidance He has already given. The request names the heart because a person may know the path and still be turned from it. 'Grant us Your mercy' asks for continued care and firmness in faith, not only for knowledge of the right way. 'You are indeed the Giver of all bounties' closes by placing the gift with Allah, the Bestower. The prayer follows the warning about hearts that pursue ambiguity: the answer is to seek steadfastness and mercy from the One who guides. The believers do not treat earlier guidance as a guarantee that they no longer need to ask. Their words move from danger, to a request for help, to trust in the Giver. A heart remains in need of Allah's guidance even after it has learned the way. The next verse continues the prayer by turning to the Day on which all people will be gathered.

**Hearts That Stray from the Truth.**

Our Lord do not cause our hearts to deviate do not cause them to incline away from the truth in their desire to interpret it such as is inappropriate for us — as You caused the hearts of those others to deviate — after You have guided us after You have shown us the way to it; and give us mercy from You as a strengthening; You are the Bestower. When Allah intends to guide someone, He makes his heart tilt towards what is good and right; and when He decides to let someone go astray, He turns his heart away from the straight path. The ones firm in knowledge say, ‘O Lord, do not let our hearts move away from the truth after you have shown it to us. Our Lord, let not our hearts stray after Thou hast guided us, and give us mercy from Thee.

**Mercy and Steadfastness.**

The present verse mentions yet another excellence of theirs - that they pray for steadfastness on the right path, not for any worldly gains, but for salvation in the life-to-come. Therefore, those who are concerned about how to remain firm in their faith, they go to the source - requesting and praying Allah for steadfastness. ( O reverser of hearts, make our hearts firm on the faith chosen by You). (Lo! Thou, only Thou art the Bestower) to the believers before us; it is also said that this means: You are the Bestower of prophethood and Islam to Muhammad. Give us, from Your vast mercy, that which will guide our hearts and protect us from misguidance. And give what you give, O Lord, as Your bounty and mercy, not as the recompense for our works or the compensation for our acts of obedience! " He said, "We will finally be released from these displeasing deeds and unworthy acts of obedi ence and attach our hearts totally to His bounty and mercy."

**The Limits of Understanding.**

The correct academic and intellectual stand regarding the allegorical part of the Quran is for man to acknowledge his limitations. One should be content to have an abstract understanding of the things which cannot be grasped precisely by the senses. When, due to his imperfect sensory perception, man cannot have a total understanding of those realities, the practical approach should be not to make any attempt to determine the precise meaning in these matters. Instead, man should pray to God to save him from entanglement in fruitless discussions. He should pray to God to grant him such wisdom as will enable him to recognize his place and be content to repose his faith in those realities, without knowing all of their details. A Day is soon to come when these realities will come into full view, but it is not possible for man to comprehend them as long as he is still being put to the test in this life, by his Lord. So as for those in whose hearts there is a deviation (from the truth) they follow (only) that which is not entirely clear thereof, seeking Al-Fitnah, and seeking its Ta'wil, but none knows its Ta'wil except Allah. 'O Prophet! Tell the disbelievers' addresses the Prophet and tells him to warn his opponents. 'Soon you will be overpowered and driven to Hell' joins defeat in this world to the Hereafter. The address is pointed rather than general: it is not describing all disbelievers in all times, nor promising the same immediate event to every community. The verse brings the pattern of denial and punishment to the people being addressed. The fighting at Badr brings the warning into its historical setting: killing, captivity, and the payment of jizya are among the outcomes of defeat. The next verse points to the two armies as a sign and to the support Allah gives. It is a warning for the addressees before the final gathering, not for every era.

When the Prophet s enjoined the Jews to enter into Islam after his return from Badr they said ‘Do not fool yourself just because you killed a few men of Quraysh inexperienced and knowing nothing about fighting’ whereupon the following was revealed Say O Muhammad to the disbelievers from among the Jews ‘You shall be vanquished sa-tughlabūn or read sa-yughlabūn ‘they shall be vanquished’ in this world through being killed or taken captive and made to pay the jizya which actually took place and mustered read in both ways wa-tuhsharūna ‘you will be mustered’ or wa-yuhsharūna ‘they will be mustered’ in the Hereafter to Hell which you shall enter — an evil cradling!’ an evil resting place. Therefore, this 'overcoming' of disbelievers mentioned in the verse simply does not refer to disbelievers universally. When Allah defeated the idolaters on the day of Badr, the Jews of Medina said: 'By Allah, this is the unlettered Prophet who was announced to us by Moses and whose attribute and description we find in our Scriptures and about whom it is also mentioned that his banner will not be defeated'. On the one hand, there are all the assets of worldly comfort and grandeur, while, on the other hand, there is the caravan of truth, having no foothold in society, and no worldly interests attached to it. By Allah, if we were to fight, you will realize that we are the real thing'. **Defeat and the Final Gathering.**

"You will be defeated and gathered together to Hell, and worst indeed is that place of rest. **Hell, Punishment, and the World.**

(to Hell, and worst indeed is that place of rest) In the hereafter what they will encounter will be from the severity of the punishment by burning ḥurqa. 13.text:
'Indeed, there was a sign for you in the two armies that met in battle' points to an event as evidence, not merely a story. 'one fighting for the cause of Allah and the other in denial' distinguishes the purpose of the two sides. 'The believers saw their enemy twice their number' is the wording of the app translation; the commentaries differ over which side saw the other as twice its number, so that difference should not be silently resolved by changing the translation. 'But Allah supports with His victory whoever He wills' places victory within Allah's will, not the armies' numbers alone. 'Surely in this is a lesson for people of insight' calls the reader to understand the encounter as a sign of Allah's support and of the limits of material strength. The previous verse announced defeat for the opponents; this one recalls Badr as an event in which the promise became visible. The verse does not credit equipment or numerical strength as the decisive cause. The two armies are distinguished by cause and denial, but both remain within Allah's power. For people of insight, the event teaches that material numbers do not control victory and that a small group may receive help against a larger one. The sighting is described in more than one way: the idolaters saw the Muslims as twice their number, while the believers' sight of the larger enemy as twice their number is placed at a particular time. The app's wording remains the translation being explained; the differing viewpoints should be compared rather than silently substituted. The actual forces were unequal, and the victory of the smaller group is the sign that calls for reflection.

**The Battle and Its Sign.**

There has already been a sign an example the verb qad kāna ‘there has been’ is used to separate the statement to follow from the previous one for you in two hosts two parties that met one another in battle on the day of Badr; one company fighting in the way of God in obedience to Him namely the Prophet and his Companions who numbered three hundred and thirteen men most of them on foot with two horses six plates of armour and eight swords; and another unbelieving; they the disbelievers numbering almost a thousand saw them the Muslims twice the like of them that is more numerous than themselves as the eye sees in manifest vision witnessing; and God granted them victory despite their fewer number; for God confirms He strengthens with His help whom He will granting him victory. This verse refers to the Battle of Badr in which the disbelievers had about 1000 men, 700 camels and 100 horses, while the Muslim mujahidin were just over 300, having a total of 70 camels, 2 horses, 6 armours and 8 swords. (There was a token) a sign confirming the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ (for you) O people of Makkah (in two hosts) in two groups: that of Muhammad and that of Abu Sufyan (which met) on the Day of Badr: You had a sign for the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ in the form of two groups-that of Muhammad and that of Abu Sufyan-who met on the Day of Badr. One group (Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions) fought in obedience of Allah, and the other group consisted of unbelievers in Allah and His Messenger (Abu Sufyan and his group). Muhammad bin Ishaq bin Yasar recorded that 'Asim bin 'Umar bin Qatadah said that when the Messenger of Allah gained victory in the battle of Badr and went back to Al-Madīnah, he gathered the Jews in the marketplace of Bani Qaynuqa'. The battle of Badr in the fourteenth year of the prophethood was a worldly example of what will happen in the next world. In fact, the believers were so few in number that they were powerless.

**The Numbers Seen at Badr.**

(They saw them with their own eyes twice their number) means, the idolators thought that the Muslims were twice as many as they were, for Allah made this illusion a factor in the victory that Islam had over them. When the two camps saw each other, the Muslims thought that the idolators were twice as many as they were, so that they would trust in Allah and seek His help. The encounter was certainly strange as each combating group saw the opponent being twice its own numbers. The sighting of so many Muslims inspired awe in the hearts of the disbelievers, while Muslims who saw the disbelievers as twice of them turned to Allah more fervently. If the actual number of disbelievers which was three times more than their own were to be realized by Muslims, they may have been overawed. This state of sighting the numbers of the other group as twice its own was at a particular time. At another time each of the two combating groups felt the other one as low in numbers, as it would appear later in Surah al-Anfal. You saw with your very eyes, O Jews, that the unbelievers were twice the number of the Companions of Muhammad. When God wants an affair to be accomplished He makes many appear to be few in the eyes of one people and few to appear as many in the eyes of another people.

**Allah's Support and Victory.**

They had hopes of Allah's help, and ultimate victory, because they had placed their total trust in Allah, were steadfast and sincerely believed in the promise of Allah revealed to them in the following words: In spite of this, those who denied the truth suffered a crushing defeat and the believers achieved a decisive victory. This is a clear proof that God is always on the side of the believers. This serves as a demonstration from God that truth does not go unsupported. The believers actually saw the disbelievers as being double their real number; but Allah helped His allies. Allah gives His support to whomever He wishes. (And Allah supports with His victory whom He wills. Verily, in this is a lesson for those who understand.) meaning, this should be an example for those who have intelligence and sound comprehension. They should contemplate about Allah's wisdom, decisions and decree, that He gives victory to His believing servants in this life and on the Day the witnesses stand up to testify. In the face of such a great difference in resources, an extraordinary victory cannot be achieved without God’s succour.

**A Lesson for People of Insight.**

Surely in that which is mentioned is a lesson for people of vision those who are discerning so will you not be warned by this and become believers? (Lo! Herein) in Allah enabling Muhammad to triumph on the Day of Badr (verily is a lesson for those who have eyes) concerning Religion, i.e. the believers; it is also said that this means: it was a lesson for those who saw it with their own eyes. In that there is a lesson and a warning for those of insight to realize that the help of Allah can come to the believers even though they may be few in number; and that defeat can come to those on falsehood even though they may be great in number. To sum up, it can be safely said that making a small group of people with very little to fight against a much stronger group and score a victory, as prophesied in Makkah, is an unusual event full of lessons for the observant and the discerning. There are obvious signs in the words and deeds of the preacher that the Truth he preaches comes from God. If He covers the inner sight baṣīra of a people the sharpness of their physical eyes abṣār will not benefit them. (so that Allah might accomplish a matter already ordained.)[8:42] meaning, so that the truth and falsehood are distinguishable, and thus the word of faith prevails over disbelief and deviation, so that the believers prevail and the disbelievers are humiliated. They live by false explanations, until finally they leave for the next world, only to learn that the words in which they had taken refuge were utterly meaningless from the standpoint of reality.

14.text:
The verse begins with what people love and ends with what is kept for them, and the order is the argument. "The enjoyment of worldly desires, women, children" names the pull that is felt, and the wording puts the loving before the naming, so desire is the subject and the things are what it moves to, and the sources keep the first item first because the attraction to women is the deepest test. "treasures of gold and silver, fine horses, cattle" then names what is stored, what is ridden, and what is kept in the field, so the list runs from the household to the land and covers the wealth of the present life. "and fertile land" closes the list with the ground itself, and the commentary on the heaps of gold reads the wording as the love of the treasure and not only of what it buys, so the verse is about the hold these things have on the heart. "has been made appealing to people" turns to those who find them fair, and the wording does not name the one who made them fair, which is why the sources weigh two readings, that the adorning is from God as a test and that it comes from Satan, and they keep both because the verse does not settle it. "These are the pleasures of this worldly life" then gathers the whole list under one word and marks how long it lasts, since the comfort is taken and then goes. "but with Allah is the finest destination" ends on the contrast and leaves the better thing unnamed, so that the verse after it can set that out, and the abode with God is the one that remains. The list is given to be understood and not to be refused, and the verse that follows takes the reader from the comfort to the question of what is better than it.

**The desire for women, children, and wealth.**

(Beautified for mankind is) what people's hearts find desirable is (love of the joys (that come) from women) meaning slave women and wives (and offspring) slaves and children, (and stored up heaps) amassed wealth (of gold and silver) it is also said that this means: minted or engraved gold and silver, (and horses branded (with their mark) beautiful branded horses and grazing in pastures, (and cattle) i.e. sheep, cows and camels (and land) cultivation and cultivated lands. These desirable things include women, children, wealth (in the form of gold and silver) that is overflowing and piled up, beautiful trained horses, livestock (such as camels, cows and sheep), as well as farmlands – all of which is the enjoyment of the life of the world which lasts only for a short while. Beautified for mankind is love of lusts that which the self lusts after and calls for beautified by Satan or by God as a test — of women children stored-up heaps of gold and silver horses of mark fine horses cattle namely camels cows and sheep and tillage the cultivation of land. Adorned for people is love of appetites, like women, children, heaped-up heaps of gold and silver, horses of mark, cattle, and tillage.

**The love of the present life as a test.**

The list is not condemned for being loved. It is named as the field of a trial. Is it not that man, with love for these things in his heart, has been put to a test as to who becomes engrossed in the enjoyments of the present life and forgets the life to come, and who comes to realize the real and temporal nature of these things, shows concern for them only in proportion to his needs, and then channels all his efforts into deeds that would make his next life good and safe? God, wishing to ascertain which of His creatures are capable of rising above worldly attractions, has so willed it that man should be attracted to and find gratification in the things of this world, but at the same time be faced with the choice of clinging to them or renouncing them in favour of the unseen things of the next world. Allah tells us that He has made the love of desirable things of this world attractive to people in order to test them. The reason for this and for all evil deeds is, in fact, the love of the worldly life. This is one of Allah's many acts of wisdom to see whether the man gets swayed by the glamour of the fleeting enjoyment of things, or remembers the Creator of these things, or the man forgets the very Creator of his own being as well. Aided by this realization, does man make these things a medium through which to know and love Allah; or, is it that he would elect to get totally lost in the love for these known transitory things, and forget all about the real Master and Creator before Whom he must appear on the Last Day and account for whatever he did. If we think about it, we shall realize that it was the love for what is desirable in this mortal world which brought them out of their homes, and in this silent process, gave the world a strong and ongoing social system.

**The comfort that passes, and the abode that remains.**

(That) which is mentioned above (is comfort of the life of the world) is of benefit to people in the life of this world and then it vanishes; it is also said that this means: the joys of this world last only for as long as the stuff of any home, a bowl, a plate and the like. That which is mentioned is the comfort of the life of this world enjoyed while it lasts but then perishes; but God — with Him is the more excellent abode place of return which is Paradise and for this reason one should desire none other than this abode. In other words, it means that all these things are there simply to serve a purpose in man's mortal life in the present world and certainly not to have him fall in love with things for their own sake, for the real beauty of the experience lies in one's ultimate resort with Allah in blissful eternity enjoying what would never perish, diminish or weaken. Sometimes, the want for more money is for the purpose of spending it on acts of worship, being kind to the family, the relatives, and spending on various acts of righteousness and obedience; this behavior is praised and encouraged in the religion.

**The things made to look fair, and the love behind them.**

Allah mentions the delights that He put in this life for people, such as women and children, and He started with women, because the test with them is more tempting. Beautified for men is the love of things they covet; women, children, Qanatir Al-Muqantarah of gold and silver, branded beautiful horses (Musawwamah), cattle and fertile land. The first verse here names some of the most de-sired things and says that they have been made to look attractive and therefore, people go after them enticed by their glamour brushing aside any concerns for the life to come, if there be any. However, as for verses where such glamorization of things has been attributed to Satan - for example, (the Satan has made their deeds look attractive to them - 8:48; 16:63; 27:24; 29:38.) - there the reference is to things that are evil, religiously and rationally; or, the reference is to a false sense of adornment which is evil because it transgresses the limits set by Allah: It means that the love of dunya (worldly life or worldly enjoyments) is the main source of all errors. This is not an easy choice, for he sees that worldly acquisitions lead him to an honourable place in society.

**Children and wealth in this world, and the future that is forgotten.**

He is so engrossed in building the future of his children in this world, that he no longer remembers the fact that there is any ‘future’ beyond this present life, to which he should give thought. Making money, accumulating riches and possessing property in this world seem so estimable to him, that he fails to realize that there is any ‘wealth’ other than this, to which he should devote his life. A believer should not become attached to these things as Allah has kept the best place of return for him: the Paradise that is as wide as the heavens and the earth. All this is just to grab a share in the temporal enjoyments of the present life which has been described in these verses. Similarly, man's wealth and possessions are means of convenience for his role in this world and in the life to come - provided that they do not enter into his heart, sit there, and kill it in the process.

15.text:
The verse answers the list before it with a question addressed to the Prophet, and the answer is put in his mouth so that the asking itself is part of the address. "Say, O Prophet" marks the turn from the description of what people love to the comparison that follows, and the command places the Prophet in the position of the one who tells. "Shall I inform you of what is better than all of this" then sets the two lives side by side, and the wording keeps the comparison open, since the better thing is not described until the answer arrives. "Those mindful of Allah will have Gardens with their Lord under which rivers flow" names the ones who receive it and the gift together, and the naming of God as their Lord brings the closeness that the gardens alone would not carry. "to stay there forever" fixes the gift in time, which is where it parts from the pleasures just described, since those are enjoyed and then go. "and pure spouses" brings the companionship, and the purity is understood of both the form and the character, so nothing in them spoils the dwelling. "along with Allah, s pleasure" raises the list above everything named before it, and this last item is the one the sources treat as the greatest, since it is the approval of the Lord and not a created thing. "And Allah is All-Seeing of His servants" closes the verse on the sight of God, which keeps the promise and the warning together, since nothing done by those who fear Him is hidden and nothing claimed by anyone else is missed. The verse is placed here to answer those who look at what they can see, and the question leaves the answer with the one addressed before the description of the gardens is given.

Allah informed them of what is better when He said,. Shall I tell you about something better than those desirable things? The answer is given in the same order as the question, so the comparison stays in view. (For those who keep from evil) keep from disbelief, ascribing partners to Allah and indecencies, in reference to Abu Bakr and his fellow believers, (with their Lord, are Gardens beneath which) beneath its trees and habitations (rivers) of wine, honey, milk and water (flow, wherein they will abide for ever) they will dwell in Paradise: they shall neither die nor leave it (and pure companions) they have therein spouses who are spared menses and filth, (and contentment from Allah) and the contentment of Allah is far greater than the bliss they enjoy.
